prompt.context: The client is a private equity firm looking to acquire a chain of car washes in the United States. The car wash chain provides basic coin-operated, self-wash services for $5, has 200 locations in 14 markets and had revenues of $40M last year. The firm is targeting 30% revenue growth in 1 year to justify the acquisition.
prompt.question: How would you think about whether or not this is attainable?

clarifying_info.q: Has the chain already tried to grow sales in its existing locations?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, increasing sales of existing products and services in existing markets has already been explored and is not a viable option.

exhibits.title: Existing Markets and Competitors
exhibits.shows: A map or table showing the car wash chain's 14 existing markets, their relative market share within each market, and the presence of competing national chains in those markets.
exhibits.data: 14 markets; market share rankings by market; presence or absence of other national chain competitors; geographic concentration in Southeast and Pacific Northwest

framework: 1. Existing locations — a. New products/services (customer demand) — b. Increase price (price sensitivity) — c. Change car wash hours — d. Marketing (advertising, partnerships, social media)
2. New locations — a. Existing markets — b. New markets (competition and response)
3. Risks — a. Cannibalization / saturation — b. Over-extended management — c. Cost implications (note: primary concern is revenue)

questions.prompt: What do you think is the size of the car wash market as a whole in the United States?
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate total US car wash market via: number of vehicles × washes per year × price per wash. Reasonable assumptions should drive the answer; the exact number matters less than logical structure.

math.setup: US households × cars per household → total vehicles; add commercial/industrial fleet; multiply by estimated wash frequency and average price
steps: Assume ~20 washes per vehicle per year

questions.prompt: Give Exhibit 1: Look at the following slide on their existing 14 markets and competitors in those markets. What do you gather from it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) the chain holds highest market share in ~10 of 14 markets (mostly major cities) with limited national competition — potential for continued expansion via organic growth, acquiring local chains, or driving out competitors; (2) geographic concentration in Southeast and Pacific Northwest means major markets in Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, and Southwest are untapped. Follow-ups: pros/cons of acquisition vs. organic build; factors for selecting expansion markets.

questions.prompt: What new products or services could the car wash company offer to grow their revenues?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm services tiered by feasibility. Most feasible: additional wash-line upgrades (wax, polish, undercarriage, detailing), coin-operated vacuums, retail convenience items. Medium feasibility: gas station add-on, basic vehicle maintenance (oil changes, tire replacements), pick-up/drop-off. Least feasible: coin-operated pet-washing area, franchise fast food (e.g., Dunkin Donuts, Subway).

questions.prompt: After considering some of your ideas, the team has the following information: people vacuum their cars half as often as they wash them when the price to vacuum is $0.50. Low-frequency customers are willing to pay $3 for wax services, while high-frequency customers are willing to pay only $1 for wax services. How much additional revenue would adding vacuums and waxing generate, and can the 30% growth target be met?
questions.guidance: Candidate needs to ask for (or be given) frequency/revenue split: low-frequency = 10x/year, 25% of revenues; high-frequency = 30x/year, 75% of revenues. Should calculate incremental revenue from vacuums and from wax at each price point, then compare total uplift to the $12M target (30% of $40M).

math.setup: Current revenue = $40M. Target growth = 30% = $12M. Calculate (a) vacuum revenue and (b) wax revenue at $3 (low-freq only) and at $1 (all customers).
steps: Wax at $3 (low-freq only): $40M × 25% = $10M low-freq revenue → $10M ÷ $5 = 2M low-freq washes → 2M × $3 = $6M
Wax at $1 (all customers, high uptake): $40M × 20% effective uplift = $8M (all customers use it because price is low)
Best combo — vacuums ($2M) + wax at $1 ($8M) = $10M incremental, only ~25% growth
Vacuums ($2M) + wax at $3 ($6M) = $8M incremental, only ~20% growth
Neither combination alone reaches the $12M (30%) target
math.answer: Adding vacuums ($0.50) and waxing at $1 yields ~$10M incremental revenue = ~25% growth, falling 5% short of the 30% target. Further growth levers (new markets, new locations) are needed to close the gap.

brainstorming.prompt: What new products or services could the car wash company offer to grow their revenues?

categories.name: Most feasible / strong precedent
ideas: Add premium wash-line tiers: wax, polish, undercarriage wash, detailing
Install coin-operated vacuums in a self-serve area after the car wash
Add a retail sales area selling air fresheners, seat covers, and convenience items

categories.name: Medium feasibility / some precedent
ideas: Add a gas station or basic vehicle maintenance services (oil changes, tire replacements) at larger locations
Offer pick-up and drop-off car wash services

categories.name: Least feasible / weak precedent
ideas: Install coin-operated hoses for a gated pet-washing area (competing with Petco)
Add a franchise fast food restaurant (e.g., Dunkin Donuts, Subway)

recommendation: Proceed with evaluating the acquisition: the chain can achieve ~25% revenue growth through adding coin-operated vacuums and waxing services to existing locations, and there is a credible path to closing the remaining 5% gap through geographic expansion or market-share gains.
The target is market leader in ~10 of 14 current markets and is entirely absent from major regions (Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, Southwest), representing significant untapped growth.
risks: Entering markets with strong existing competitors could be difficult and costly
Driving competitors out of existing markets risks triggering a price war
Cost of adding new services must be analyzed to confirm net revenue benefit
Over-extended management from rapid geographic expansion
next_steps: Research potential new markets (Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, Southwest) to quantify expansion opportunity
Dive deeper into existing markets to assess organic growth potential and viability of acquiring local chains
Conduct cost analysis of adding vacuum and wax services to validate net margin impact
Discuss acquisition price relative to identified growth potential
